15873.heading: Conclusion
15873.content:
Also known as an output in a logical system

In a [[Valid Argument]], the conclusion must be true in every case where all of the premises are true. A conclusion can therefore follow validly from premises without being asserted as independently true.

15876.title: Conditional Breakpoint
15876.heading: Conditional Breakpoint
15876.content:
A conditional breakpoint pauses execution only when a specified expression or hit-count condition is satisfied. It is useful when a line runs many times but only one state or iteration is relevant to the fault.

The condition is evaluated when execution reaches the ordinary [[Breakpoint]] location. This reduces repeated manual continuation and preserves the state of the interesting case for inspection.

15882.title: Concept Stage
15882.heading: Concept Stage
15882.content:
The concept stage is the first major stage of game design. It turns an idea into a stable outline of the player, platform, genre, business context, and central experience.

Its result should guide later work without specifying every detail. Decisions that define the identity and feasibility of the project are established here so the [[Elaboration Stage]] can explore how to realize them.

15885.title: Conceptual Model
15885.heading: Conceptual Model
15885.content:
A conceptual model is a person's understanding of the information and tasks that make up a system. It can be informal and incomplete because it represents an understanding rather than the system itself.

The designer's model is the relatively complete view formed during development and may include task analyses, diagrams, and implementation knowledge. The user's model is built from experience with the interface. For high [[Usability]], the system should communicate the designer's model clearly enough that the user's model becomes accurate.

Consistent behavior, visible system state, [[Feedback]], and [[Affordance]]s help align the two models.

Games make this alignment dynamic: the [[Game Model]] changes in response to action, while the [[Player Mental Model]] changes in response to feedback. Productive uncertainty leaves room for prediction and learning without making the game's effects seem arbitrary.

15888.title: Conceptual Clustering
15888.heading: Conceptual Clustering
15888.content:
Conceptual clustering groups observations while also building an interpretable description of each group. A concept summarizes which attribute values are predictable within the class and which values distinguish it from other classes.

COBWEB represents those concepts as nodes in an incrementally updated hierarchy. The group definition is therefore tied to an inference model, not only a geometric boundary.

15891.title: Conceptual Composition
15891.heading: Conceptual Composition
15891.content:
Conceptual composition combines the meanings of words and phrases into the meaning of a larger expression. The interpretation depends not only on individual words but also on their syntactic and semantic relationships.

An assistant uses composition to build a [[Meaning Representation]] with an [[Intent]] and linked arguments. This is harder than detecting isolated keywords because order and structure can change who did what to whom.

15894.title: Concept Statement
15894.heading: Concept Statement
15894.content:
A concept statement expresses a game's central experience and differentiator in one or two brief, accurate sentences. It should be short enough to remember and repeat while still communicating what the player does and why the game is distinctive.

The statement anchors a [[Game Concept Document]] and opens a [[Game Pitch]]. Refining it with other people reveals where the underlying concept is unclear or where listeners form a different mental model than intended.

The source calls this a high concept statement and limits it to roughly two or three sentences. Its job is to communicate the most important aspects quickly, leaving platform, audience, progression, and production detail to the larger concept document.

15897.content:

Monitoring compares later records and outcomes with the conditions under which the model was trained. A meaningful change can prompt fresh data preparation, evaluation, and retraining. 15909.title: Concave Function
15909.heading: Concave Function
15909.content:
A function is concave when its negative is a [[Convex Function]]. Its graph lies on or above the chord joining any two points in its domain.

For a differentiable concave function, a local maximum is also a global maximum. A twice-differentiable function is concave where its [[Hessian Matrix]] is negative semidefinite.

16020.content:
A computer is an agent that carries out calculations and symbol manipulations according to specified rules. The agent may be a person or a machine, although electronic computers perform long sequences much faster and with less distraction than human computers.

Calling a machine a computational agent does not imply understanding or intelligence. Its reliable behavior depends on representations, programs, and physical mechanisms designed by people.

16023.title: Computer
16023.heading: Computer
16023.content:
A computer is a human or machine that performs calculations and symbol manipulations according to precisely specified rules. Before electronic machines, the word commonly named a person trained to carry out long computations.

An automatic computer performs those rules through physical mechanisms without ongoing human intervention. Speed and repeatability distinguish the machine, but meaning and purpose still come from the people who design and use its computations.

Computer-supported cooperative work studies how computer systems can support collaborative activities and their coordination.

Collaboration contexts can be classified by time and place. Participants may work synchronously or asynchronously, and they may be collocated or remote. These dimensions affect the communication, awareness, and coordination mechanisms the system must provide.

CSCW is closely related to [[Social Computing]]. In a shared [[Virtual Environment]], it may use [[Telepresence]] so participants in different physical locations can work in the same spatial task area.

16029.title: Computer Mouse
16029.heading: Computer Mouse
16029.content:
A computer mouse converts hand movement and button presses into selection and positioning on a graphical display. Douglas Engelbart developed the device while investigating ways to augment human intellect.

The mouse made pointing at visible interface objects faster than typing many commands. Its design links fine motor control to direct manipulation of digital representations.

16032.title: Computer Worm
16032.heading: Computer Worm
16032.content:
A computer worm is self-contained [[Independent Malware]] that copies itself between systems, commonly by exploiting network reachability or software weaknesses. Unlike a [[Computer Virus]], it does not need to attach to a host file to propagate.

Autonomous replication can create rapid, large-scale effects even when damage is not the only objective. The [[Worm Component Model]] highlights the targeting, propagation, activation, and payload functions that enable this spread.

16035.title: Computer Virus
16035.heading: Computer Virus
16035.content:
A computer virus is malicious code that attaches to a host and reproduces by infecting additional files or programs when the host executes. Unlike a [[Computer Worm]], it generally depends on a carrier and some action that activates or transfers the infected host.

The [[Virus Component Model]] separates replication, triggering, and payload behavior, making clear that a virus's method of spreading is distinct from the harmful action it eventually performs.

16038.title: Computer Operator
16038.heading: Computer Operator
16038.content:
A computer operator manages the physical and procedural flow of jobs through a shared installation. Duties historically included mounting tapes, feeding card decks, handling printers, and responding to machine conditions.

Operators controlled access to expensive mainframes while programmers and end users remained outside the computer room. Interactive systems later automated or redistributed much of this intermediary work.

16041.title: Computer Network
16041.heading: Computer Network
16041.content:
A computer network is a set of computational or navigational devices connected by channels that let them exchange information. The set can be small or arbitrarily large, and its nodes do not need to share one hardware type or operating system.

Network software must therefore communicate through defined messages rather than assume access to the remote device's memory or implementation. Distribution introduces latency, partial failure, security boundaries, and asynchronous behavior that are absent from a purely local call.

Computer literacy courses teach people to use common digital tools such as word processors and spreadsheets. They can improve practical access but offer little understanding of how computation, programs, and information systems work.

For computational-thinking advocates, literacy was too shallow to prepare students to shape a digital world. Its limited appeal helped motivate later movements toward computational fluency and programming.

16047.title: Computational Unsolvability
16047.heading: Computational Unsolvability
16047.content:
A problem is computationally unsolvable when no algorithm can produce the required correct answer for every permitted input. This is a limit on computability itself, not merely on available time, memory, or engineering skill.

The [[Halting Problem]] supplies the central example. Similar questions about whether programs halt on all inputs, agree on every input, or ever halt from a blank configuration inherit the same kind of impossibility.

16050.title: Computer Immunology
16050.heading: Computer Immunology
16050.content:
Computer immunology applies ideas from biological immune systems to cyber defense. Instead of relying only on a fixed list of known threats, a system can distinguish expected activity from harmful change, remember prior encounters, and coordinate a response.

The analogy motivates the [[Self-Nonself Security Model]], [[Security Memory of Prior Infections]], and [[Autonomic Security System]]. It is a design framework: computing systems must translate biological functions into measurable technical signals and controlled actions.

This level cannot be reduced to a short list of classroom concepts. It is cultivated through sustained practice, including learning when to use an abstraction, when to inspect physical details, and when a proposed computation cannot safely do the job.

16068.content:
Computational thinking requires humility about what computers can understand and accomplish. Machines execute specified operations quickly, but they do not supply the meaning of their inputs or automatically correct mistakes that their designers failed to anticipate.

Humility also means recognizing impossible and intractable problems, the need for domain knowledge, and the risks created when speed amplifies an error. It turns limits into design constraints instead of hiding them behind claims that every problem is computational.

Computational thinking also explains phenomena by interpreting them as information processes. A scientist may ask what transformations, states, or exchanges could reproduce an observed process, then investigate that interpretation through a [[Computational Model]].

This explanatory face does not require claiming that nature literally is a computer. It treats computation as a productive lens for forming models, running [[Simulation|simulations]], and discovering patterns that theory or experiment alone may not reveal.

16074.heading: Computational Thinking Beyond Sequential Steps
16074.content:
Many definitions of computational thinking assume a von Neumann machine that executes a sequence of instructions. Emerging systems can compute through energy minimization, chemical evolution, or learned signal transformations without presenting a programmer with an ordered instruction list.

A broader definition focuses on designing computations and interpreting information processes. It can include new machines while still requiring explicit representations, controllable setup, and a way to interpret results.

16077.heading: Computational Thinking as Computational Design
16077.content:
Computational thinking includes the practiced ability to design computations that let a [[Computer]] perform a valuable job. It joins an understanding of [[Algorithm|algorithms]], representations, and machines with judgment about whether the resulting system will work reliably in its actual setting.

This design face is broader than writing code. It asks how a desired capability can be made machine-realizable, how errors and limits will be handled, and how the result will serve the people who depend on it.

16080.content:
Computational task decomposition breaks a large calculation into smaller pieces that separate workers or processors can execute. The pieces must have explicit inputs, outputs, and ordering relationships so their intermediate results can be recombined correctly.

Decomposition creates opportunities for [[Parallel Computation]] and distributed work, but it also creates communication and coordination costs. A good partition balances independent work against the messages required between parts.

16086.heading: Computational Model Ambiguity Across Fields
16086.content:
The term computational model has different meanings across disciplines. In science it often denotes equations describing a physical process; in computer science it often denotes an abstract machine capable of executing programs.

Collaboration improves when participants make the intended meaning explicit. A scientific model may be implemented by a simulation running on an abstract machine, linking the two senses without making them identical.

16089.title: Computational Model
16089.heading: Computational Model
16089.content:
A computational model can describe an abstract machine that executes programs or a mathematical representation of a process that a computer can evaluate. Its meaning depends on whether the context is computer science or a scientific domain.

In simulation, the senses meet: equations representing a phenomenon are translated into the states and operations of an executable machine. The model’s assumptions determine what the resulting computation can legitimately explain.

Computational fluid dynamics represents the space around an object with a three-dimensional mesh and approximates airflow equations at its points. Mesh cells are made smaller where flow changes rapidly, such as near an aircraft surface.

A supercomputer advances the field through time and visualization converts numerical values into interpretable patterns of flow and stress. The method can reduce dependence on wind tunnels and physical test flights.

16095.title: Computational Fluency
16095.heading: Computational Fluency
16095.content:
Computational fluency combines practical capability with concepts and skills for expressing ideas through information technology. It goes beyond operating applications toward adapting tools, understanding systems, and creating computational artifacts.

The fluency movement offered a richer educational goal than literacy but did not by itself produce universal computing courses. Its concepts nevertheless helped prepare the later computational-thinking movement.

16098.title: Computational Complexity
16098.heading: Computational Complexity
16098.content:
Computational complexity describes the resources an [[Algorithm]] requires as the size of its input grows. The principal resources are [[Time Complexity|time]], represented by the number of elementary operations, and [[Space Complexity|space]], represented by required storage.

The purpose is to compare algorithms independently of a particular computer. Hardware changes the duration of one operation, but it does not change whether the number of operations grows linearly, quadratically, exponentially, or according to another complexity family.

Computational exploration uses models and simulations to investigate a phenomenon when analytical solutions or direct experiments are insufficient. Researchers vary conditions, visualize behavior, and search for recurrences that suggest new explanations.

The activity differs from merely calculating a known answer. It treats computation as an environment for discovery while requiring scientific judgment about which simulated patterns deserve confidence.

16122.title: Compound Linear Inequality
16122.heading: Compound Linear Inequality
16122.content:
A compound linear inequality combines more than one linear constraint. An "and" relationship requires values satisfying both constraints and therefore uses their intersection. An "or" relationship accepts values satisfying either constraint and uses their union.

Each component can be solved separately with the ordinary sign rules, then the solution sets are combined. A chained form such as (-1\leq x<2) describes one bounded interval with different endpoint types. A disjoint "or" condition may produce two rays rather than one interval, so graphing helps reveal the final structure.

A composition series is a finite chain 0 = M₀ ⊊ M₁ ⊊ ··· ⊊ Mₖ = M in which every quotient Mᵢ/Mᵢ₋₁ is a [[Simple Module]].

The number k is the [[Module Length]]. If one composition series exists, every composition series has the same length, and every submodule chain can be extended to one.
